Today, on International Women’s Day, we are reminded of the promises world leaders made 30 years ago in Beijing to deliver rights, equality and empowerment #ForAllWomenAndGirls
 
A key part of realizing these promises is ensuring a just and equitable energy transition. Sustainable energy and gender equality are deeply intertwined, yet key challenges persist in advancing both:
 
➡️ Energy poverty goes beyond being an infrastructure issue - it is a gendered crisis. On average, women and girls in Africa spend 50 hours a week collecting firewood, water and cooking – time that could be spent on education, improving livelihoods and health.🌐
 
➡️ Women are more than energy consumers – they are agents of change as energy producers, innovators and decision makers. 🙏
 
While the benefits of an inclusive and diverse workforce are clear, the gender divide in the energy sector persists. Women make up only 20% of the energy workforce, despite making up 40% of workers globally. Women-led startups receive less than 3% of energy investment capital.
 
Investing in women-led initiatives and empowering women as leaders in the energy sector can drive solutions for the just transition. ⚡️
 
2025 is a critical year for the gender-energy nexus. Milestones including CSW69 and COP30 present key moments for accelerated action. While #SDG7 is one of only six SDGs without gender-specific indicators, this should be no excuse not to scale up action towards achieving a gender-responsive just transition!
 
Now is the time to invest in women-led energy initiatives, advocate for gender-responsive energy policies, and support women’s leadership in the energy sector.

Not just on #IWD, but every day.
 
#SustainableEnergy #GenderEquality #IWD2025 #CSW69

Not long ago, the energy sector was almost entirely male-dominated. Today, things are changing. 

Women now make up 32% of the renewable energy workforce, a significant step forward compared to traditional energy, where we are still at 22%. 

The sustainable energy revolution is not only transforming the way the world is powered—it is also creating new opportunities for us. By 2030, 18 million new clean energy jobs will be created. The question is not whether women have a place in this sector—we are already here. From leading solar initiatives in rural communities to driving innovation, advancing science, and shaping energy diplomacy, we are building the future.

But progress does not mean the work is done. Women-led startups still receive less than 3% of energy investment capital, and in many regions, women spend up to 50 hours a week gathering firewood instead of pursuing education or employment.

The transition is already happening, but it must be fair and inclusive. Creating an equitable environment at all decision-making levels is not just about fairness—it is an opportunity to unlock potential and ensure that the future truly belongs to everyone, through a just energy transition.

We have come a long way—now let’s go further. Not just today, but every day. #IWD #WomenInEnergy #SustainableFuture #JustTransition UNDP Sustainable Energy Hub Riad Meddeb Ana Victoria Rojas

⚡️From Local Action to Global Investment: Highlights from the Second Half of the 20th Annual Columbia Energy Symposium⚡️

Last Friday afternoon at the 20th Annual Columbia Energy Symposium was an energizing exploration into the financial and policy dimensions of our energy future.

The session opened with an impactful keynote by Shawyn Howard, 30th Mayor of the City of Mount Vernon, who underscored the critical role local governments play in climate action. She stressed that a data-driven narrative is essential for securing funding and urged us to engage directly with communities, through schools, local organizations, and religious spaces, to foster sustainable solutions.

In Panel Discussion 3, "Financing the Energy Transition in Emerging and Developing Markets," moderated by Muriel Jacques, Diego Mesa, Riad Meddeb, Luisa Palacios, and Suman Sureshbabu examined the challenges of high capital costs and policy barriers in developing markets. Their discussion charted a course toward unlocking the immense renewable potential in emerging markets through innovative financing approaches, risk-sharing mechanisms, and scalable investment models.

Panel Discussion 4, "Unlocking Energy Transition Through Private Capital," moderated by Heather Hartel, brought together Neil Suslak, Mekala Krishnan, Christopher Poirier, and Daniel Egan to explore how private capital can drive innovation and development of clean energy systems—reinforcing the notion that energy underpins every economic process.

The afternoon wrapped up with a stand-up live show by Rollie Williams and Matt Nelsen of Climate Town, who mixed humor with insight to tackle misinformation on wind farms and fossil fuels, ending the day on a thoughtful and uplifting note.

A heartfelt thank you to all our speakers, panelists, moderators, and the engaged audience for making the symposium's second half as inspiring and impactful as it was dynamic!

Stay tuned for more updates and insights from the Symposium here and on our Instagram (https://lnkd.in/eSwMxnG5).

How do we solve the energy access paradox? ⚡  
 
This week, leaders at the 2025 Sustainable Energy for All Global Forum tackle this pressing question.  
 
Over 658 million people still lack electricity — 571 million in Sub-Saharan Africa alone. The regional divide is growing. Yet sustainable energy is more than a commodity; it’s key to realizing development and human rights by powering education, health, livelihoods, food and water security and more.  
 
The opportunities are clear. Universal energy access in Sub-Saharan Africa could create 4 million jobs by 2030, while technological advances make sustainable electricity the most cost-effective solution. In a time of growing geopolitical tensions, sustainable energy offers a pathway to energy independence. 
 
We know the solutions. Closing the gap by 2030 requires $30 billion annually, with half of the investments needed in Sub-Saharan Africa. Driving large-scale electrification requires unlocking technological solutions and focusing on de-risking policy and finance to attract private capital. 
 
The world cannot afford to leave 658 million people in the dark. 
 
💡 Our latest Sustainable Energy Bulletin explores the path to bridging the gap, latest trends, and key opportunities ahead 👉 https://bit.ly/4bKL5Dj

I had the pleasure to participate in the “Small Islands, Big Solutions” roundtable discussion for SIDS at the #SEforALLForum.🇧🇧 
 The Antigua and Barbuda Agenda for SIDS outlined the clear priority of placing sustainable energy at the center of development. With SIDS currently spending 5-10% of their GDP on fossil fuel imports, this Ministerial reminds us that: sustainable, reliable, and affordable energy must be the engine of resilience and economic growth in SIDS.🏝️

 With many SIDS already on track to achieve a 100% renewable energy power mix by 2030, this is not only about infrastructure; it’s about sovereignty and unlocking just development opportunities. Beyond ambition, we need concrete pathways to impact. 

 1️⃣ Unlock scaled and concessional finance: We need financing mechanisms that work for SIDS not against them, to reach the $5.9 billion needed annually to meet 2030 targets.

 2️⃣️ Scale SIDS-specific digital technologies: AI, smart grids, and geospatial tools can accelerate energy access & enhance resilience for SIDS. 

 3️⃣ Beyond technology and finance: We need to create enabling policy environments & strategic partnerships, especially through SIDS-SIDS cooperation. 

We are committed to driving a future where SIDS are not defined by vulnerability, but as leaders in clean, resilient, and digital societies. Let us rise up for SIDS in their sustainable energy revolution!🏝️⚡️

With her magnetic personality, Prime Minister Mia Mottley has set a down-to-earth tone for the Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL) Global Forum in Barbados, which concluded yesterday. Here are some of my take aways:

(1) There is no shortage of capital for energy access - a literal quote from an investor: 'there may even be too much concessional capital floating around'
(2) There is no shortage of entrepreneurs and developers - the venue was buzzing with startups or established businesses across the value chain, from solar lanterns, clean cookstoves to utility scale PV and everything in between
(3) There is no shortage of ambition, as Andrew Herscowitz repeatedly mentioned, the #mission300 initiative aims to connect 300 million people by 2030 by bringing many development partners together.
(4) There is no shortage of 'action', there is a lot of healthy trial and error in this space, a lot of success being celebrated, but also a lot of failure swept under the rug. More structured thinking about investment risks, risk mitigation and financing costs would help governments be better prepared for action. Grateful to Riad Meddeb for the opportunity to discuss about the UNDP's role on that front. 
(5) There is an acute shortage of evidence on what works and under what conditions. Even for the most intuitive relationships, for example between electricity and income generation or quality of education, the evidence is very weak. We are trying to play our part with the work we are doing with Norad - Norwegian Agency for Development Cooperation and Endre Ottosen on the evidence base for clean energy interventions. 
(6) There is a (temporary?) shortage of solutions for major issues like currency risk or crowding in versus crowding out of private capital, and others. Promising work and ideas from Wale Shonibare!
(7) Above all, there is a shortage of patience and realism, understanding that certain processes take time, that the issues in the energy sector cannot be insulated from other structural issues at the country level, that affordability problems cannot always be solved with market solutions, that some interventions are worth while even if they can't produce immediate measurable results. 

All in all, a remarkable event, congrats to Damilola Ogunbiyi Stefano Marguccio Divyam Nagpal and all the SE4All team!

Achieving Mission 300 requires a fundamental shift in how we approach Energy Access!⚡️ 

Yesterday, in a timely and critical session organized by The World Bank  and ESMAP - Energy Sector Management Assistance Program  - Energy Sector Management Assistance Program at the #SEforALLForum in Barbados, we discussed what it will take to scale distributed renewable energy and unlock financing to reach 300 million people by 2030: 

1️⃣ Distributed renewables must be embedded in national energy strategies: Clear interconnection policies are critical to ensuring mini-grids can complement, rather than compete with, national grids. When integrated effectively, they could provide up to 11% of new electricity connections. 

2️⃣ The cost of capital is a barrier to scaling clean energy: High borrowing costs and debt burdens are locking out investment. Policy and financial de-risking mechanisms, including debt-for-energyswaps and financial instruments, must be expanded. 

3️⃣ A whole-of-society approach is essential: Civil society, local leadership, and communities must be at the center of designing and scaling energy solutions, as seen in Guinea’s successful decentralized projects. 

Technology alone will not deliver M300. Policy and regulatory reforms, coupled with strategic financing, are needed to turn solutions into large-scale impact.🌐

UNDP  and United Nations Capital Development Fund (UNCDF)  are connecting policy, finance, and innovation to drive transformation. We are moving beyond business-as-usual approaches and rethinking financing clean energy to drive meaningful and lasting development impact. 

Through initiatives like the Africa Minigrids Program, Solar for Health, and financial de-risking instruments, we are committed to scale clean energy through collaboration!🤝⚡️
#EnergyForDevelopment #SEforALLForum #SustainableFinance #EnergyTransition

Powering the SDGs: From Connections to Consumption.💡

By 2050, the global population will grow by nearly 2 billion, driving electricity demand up by nearly 50%. While clean energy generation is on track to break new records over the 2025-2027 forecast period (with renewable capacity projected to triple by 2030) a critical question remains: how do people access energy? 

Yesterday at the at the #SEforALLForum, we gathered with an excellent group of experts -  Sarah Malm  (Gogla), Cassady Walters  (Rockefeller Foundation/GEAPP), Alexander Obiechina  Ltd), and Martijn Veen  (SNV) - to explore this pressing concern and discuss how finance, decentralized solutions, and innovation can unlock an inclusive, affordable, and productive energy future. 

Achieving universal electrification by 2030 requires $52 billion per year: but finance alone isn’t the answer. To close this gap, we must: 

➡️ Shift our focus from generating energy, to delivering it to people affordably, efficiently and securely. 

➡️ Link decentralized renewable energy solutions with productive uses that unlock a pathway to inclusive growth and improved livelihoods, creating a spiral of positive development outcomes. 

➡️ Increase energy storage capacity to accommodate new variable, context specific, renewable energy generation. 

➡️ Revolutionize our energy supply by harnessing AI to optimize energy storage systems. 

While we have made significant progress in energy generation, we are reminded that technology alone will not get us to our goals. With 685 million people still living without electricity, our work is far from over.  

We need innovative financial models, inclusive business strategies, and above all else, a commitment to leaving no one behind!☀️🤝⚡️
#EnergyForDevelopment  #EnergyAccess #RenewableEnergy #SustainableDevelopment

Today, I joined fellow experts and practitioners at the Think7 Summit panel on "Energy Security and Climate", hosted by the Centre for International Governance Innovation (CIGI).
 
Climate change and energy security are deeply interlinked. While the global energy system fuels development, it also drives climate change, accounting for 75% of greenhouse gas emissions. As climate change intensifies, the links with energy security deepen. With conflicts, debt, and rising inequalities straining economies, the G7 has a strategic opportunity to support a just, inclusive energy transition that ensures no one is left behind:
 
➡️ Energy security is climate resilience. Despite record growth in renewables, climate disruptions in 2023 slashed wind energy output by up to 30% and hydropower by over 50% in some regions. Our energy systems must be designed for the climate of today - not the past.
 
➡️ Securing energy means rethinking how and where we invest. Over 90% of clean energy growth is in advanced economies and China, while SIDS face climate losses up to 9% of GDP and unsustainable debt. Through innovative tools like Debt Swaps for Energy, UNDP is helping unlock renewable investment - turning fiscal constraints into opportunities for resilience.
 
➡️ Digital, data, and AI are the new core of energy infrastructure. With electricity demand set to double by 2050, climate intelligence - from predictive models to smart grids - is essential to build resilient, investable, and future-ready energy systems.
 
Now is the time for the G7 to move from ambition to implementation. With 1.18 billion people still living in energy poverty, energy security must drive human development through partnerships, stronger Global South-North cooperation and targeted investment.
 
Thank you to CIGI and fellow panelists for a timely, forward-looking discussion.
 
#T7CIGI #T72025 #Think7CIGI #EnergyforDevelopment #EnergyTransition

Electric utopia or elite privilege? Rethinking e-mobility for the Global South🚗⚡
 
The future of mobility is electric - but is it truly global? In 2023, nearly one in five vehicles sold worldwide was electric, and by 2035 electric vehicles are projected to make up almost 50% of the global auto market. However, a staggering 95% of EV sales are concentrated in China, Europe, and the United States.
 
While the Global South remains largely on the sidelines, accounting for only a small fraction of these sales, the shift to e-mobility holds immense potential. It presents an opportunity to:
 
✅ Improve air quality and health outcomes, particularly in the Global South, where air pollution claims millions of lives, accounting for 89% of the 4.2 million premature deaths annually.
 
✅ Reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels, enhancing energy security and economic resilience.
 
✅ Electrify shared and public transport, ensuring affordable and inclusive mobility solutions, revitalizing a form of widely affordable transportation essential for last-mile connectivity.
 
✅ Create jobs and foster economic growth, as EV manufacturing alone is expected to create 1.5 million new jobs by 2030.
 
Despite solutions emerging, such as innovative financing models; digital technologies; and localized electrification strategies, the question remains: how can the Global South harness the e-mobility revolution to drive sustainable development and climate action?
 
I invite you all to explore these insights and the opportunities that lie ahead for the Global South to transition to e-mobility in my latest illuminem article: https://lnkd.in/dEQ62xiy

Delighted to have joined colleagues from @UNDP Bhutan on their webinar co-organized by @Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources to explore Bhutan’s green hydrogen potential.
 
In 2023, the world produced 97 million tons of hydrogen - but less than 1% came from low-emission sources. The momentum is growing, but the challenge is clear: how we choose to develop green hydrogen, and for whom, will define whether it delivers on its promise:

1️⃣ Green hydrogen must be a tool for development - not just decarbonization. With youth unemployment at 28.6% and 55% of the population living in rural areas, Bhutan needs growth that is inclusive and job-rich. Green hydrogen could support this, if linked to skills development, rural infrastructure, and the broader vision of Gross National Happiness.

2️⃣ Sustainability is not one-size-fits-all. While Bhutan has vast hydropower resources, green hydrogen production raises concerns about water use, land access, and biodiversity. It takes 9 litres of water to produce 1 kg of hydrogen. In a mountainous country, with seasonal water stress, these trade-offs matter. The goal must be to balance ambition with realism, scale with sustainability.

3️⃣ The transition must be just and equitable. That means ensuring benefits reach everyone. We should avoid extractive investment models and prioritize policies that keep value local, empower communities, and protect natural and cultural heritage.
 
@UNDP remains committed to supporting Bhutan's green hydrogen journey: not as champions of a single solution, but as partners dedicated to inclusive long-term impact.
 
For Bhutan, a whole-of-society approach is key. A just energy transition is not only about technology - it’s about ensuring that the benefits of innovation reach everyone, with inclusion at its core. Watch here 👉🏾 https://lnkd.in/ej-_kr3H
 
Thank you to colleagues and fellow panelists for a timely, forward-looking discussion.

Today, I joined fellow experts and practitioners at the Think7 Summit panel on "Energy Security and Climate", hosted by the Centre for International Governance Innovation (CIGI).
 
Climate change and energy security are deeply interlinked. While the global energy system fuels development, it also drives climate change, accounting for 75% of greenhouse gas emissions. As climate change intensifies, the links with energy security deepen. With conflicts, debt, and rising inequalities straining economies, the G7 has a strategic opportunity to support a just, inclusive energy transition that ensures no one is left behind:
 
➡️ Energy security is climate resilience. Despite record growth in renewables, climate disruptions in 2023 slashed wind energy output by up to 30% and hydropower by over 50% in some regions. Our energy systems must be designed for the climate of today - not the past.
 
➡️ Securing energy means rethinking how and where we invest. Over 90% of clean energy growth is in advanced economies and China, while SIDS face climate losses up to 9% of GDP and unsustainable debt. Through innovative tools like Debt Swaps for Energy, UNDP is helping unlock renewable investment - turning fiscal constraints into opportunities for resilience.
 
➡️ Digital, data, and AI are the new core of energy infrastructure. With electricity demand set to double by 2050, climate intelligence - from predictive models to smart grids - is essential to build resilient, investable, and future-ready energy systems.
 
Now is the time for the G7 to move from ambition to implementation. With 1.18 billion people still living in energy poverty, energy security must drive human development through partnerships, stronger Global South-North cooperation and targeted investment.
 
Thank you to CIGI and fellow panelists for a timely, forward-looking discussion. #T7CIGI #T72025 #Think7CIGI #EnergyforDevelopment #EnergyTransition

Electric utopia or elite privilege? Rethinking e-mobility for the Global South🚗⚡
 
The future of mobility is electric - but is it truly global? In 2023, nearly one in five vehicles sold worldwide was electric, and by 2035 electric vehicles are projected to make up almost 50% of the global auto market. However, a staggering 95% of EV sales are concentrated in China, Europe, and the United States.
 
While the Global South remains largely on the sidelines, accounting for only a small fraction of these sales, the shift to e-mobility holds immense potential. It presents an opportunity to:
 
✅ Improve air quality and health outcomes, particularly in the Global South, where air pollution claims millions of lives, accounting for 89% of the 4.2 million premature deaths annually.
 
✅ Reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels, enhancing energy security and economic resilience.
 
✅ Electrify shared and public transport, ensuring affordable and inclusive mobility solutions, revitalizing a form of widely affordable transportation essential for last-mile connectivity.
 
✅ Create jobs and foster economic growth, as EV manufacturing alone is expected to create 1.5 million new jobs by 2030.
 
Despite solutions emerging, such as innovative financing models; digital technologies; and localized electrification strategies, the question remains: how can the Global South harness the e-mobility revolution to drive sustainable development and climate action?

⚡ Energy is a fundamental enabler of development — and nowhere is this more evident than in the health sector. It delivers one of the highest returns in climate adaptation, yet remains critically underfunded.

🔌 1 in 4 health facilities globally lacks electricity, and at least 25,000 in sub-Saharan Africa operate with no electricity access. Bridging this gap requires four strategic shifts:

✅ Integrating Sustainable Energy into Health Policies and Planning
Nearly 1 billion people rely on health facilities without reliable electricity. Energy must be integrated into health strategies and Universal Health Coverage (UHC) planning.

✅ Financing Sustainable Energy for Health Resilience
An estimated $4.9 billion is needed to electrify facilities in 63 low- and middle-income countries. Funding should prioritize decentralized renewable energy as core health infrastructure.

✅ Promoting Data-driven Decisionmaking
In 46 low- and middle-income countries, 60% of health facilities face unreliable power. Energy audits, monitoring, geospatial data, and AI-powered storage can improve reliability.

✅ Prioritizing Sustainable Energy in Fragile and Crisis-affected Settings
With 2 billion people in conflict-affected areas, solar mini-grids and Pay-As-You-Go models ensure care continues when the grid fails.

Investing in sustainable energy is not just about powering facilities — it’s about powering health systems that save lives.

Closing Africa’s Energy Access Gap: Looking Beyond the Traditional Grid to a Decentralized Future.🌍⚡️
 
The global energy access gap is widening, and it is increasingly a challenge for countries in Sub-Saharan Africa. Of the 685 million people globally without electricity, 571 million live in Sub-Saharan Africa.
 
Grid expansion alone will not close Africa’s energy access gap.
 
Decentralized Renewable Energy (DRE) solutions, such as solar mini-grids and off-grid systems, are already offering a fast and cost-effective path to electrification. Not only could they provide 80% of new electricity connections in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, but they have already provided electricity access to 560 million people worldwide. These solutions go beyond access - they have become a catalyst for change in Africa:
 
➡️ Nigeria’s market-driven approach has enabled the deployment of +100 solar-powered mini-grids.
 
➡️ Easy Solar has brought power to +1M people in Sierra Leone and Liberia since 2016.
 
➡️ Retrofitting diesel-powered irrigation system with solar energy helped mango farmers boost yields by 185% per tree in Tanzania.
 
But to be successful, governments must be proactive in planning regulatory frameworks that enable mini-grids to complement national grids rather than compete with them; as without clear interconnection policies, these projects risk becoming stranded assets. Through leveraging digitalization, AI, and advanced grid technologies, smart decentralized systems can enhance efficiency, minimize energy losses and optimize renewable energy integration to power a sustainable and inclusive energy future.⚡️♻️

⚡ Energy is a fundamental enabler of development — and nowhere is this more evident than in the health sector. It delivers one of the highest returns in climate adaptation, yet remains critically underfunded.

✅ Financing Sustainable Energy for Health Resilience

✅ Promoting Data-driven Decisionmaking
In 46 low- and middle-income countries, 60% of health facilities face unreliable power. Energy audits, monitoring, geospatial data, and AI-powered storage can improve reliability.

✅ Prioritizing Sustainable Energy in Fragile and Crisis-affected Settings
With 2 billion people in conflict-affected areas, solar mini-grids and Pay-As-You-Go models ensure care continues when the grid fails.

Investing in sustainable energy is not just about powering facilities — it’s about powering health systems that save lives.

This Earth Day 2025, we take time to reflect on the importance of the circular energy revolution. The transition to sustainable energy is more important than ever: not only for the environment but for the global economy and society as a whole.
 
Historically, the production and consumption of energy has been responsible for >75% of greenhouse gas emissions - making it the primary driver of climate change and global warming. However, sustainable energy solutions, such solar and wind power, are becoming increasingly more accessible and cost-effective. In 2023, renewables accounted for 30% of global electricity supply. By 2030, electricity is projected to grow six times faster than energy demand driven by a surge in renewable energy adoption and the rise in electric vehicles. 
 
Yet as demand for electricity and battery storage & utilization increases, so too does the need for critical minerals. While less harmful than fossil fuels, we need to also ask ourselves:
 
➡️ With battery storage capacity currently at 3TWh, anticipated to triple by 2030, what will this mean for the battery sector on the whole? How and where will this impact on the demand for critical minerals?
 
 ➡️ Extracting minerals sustainably remains a challenge, with lithium production requiring 2.2 million liters of water per ton - an immense demand in regions with limited water access. How do we ensure that we are not exacerbating as opposed to enabling human development?
 
➡️ With 54% of critical mineral reserves sitting on Indigenous People’s land, how do we ensure these actors have a voice?
 
➡️ Although Africa currently holds over 50% of global reserves and production of cobalt and manganese, which are critical components for batteries, how do we ensure that these benefits are evenly distributed amongst all members of society? 
 
While renewable electricity continues to scale up - reshaping markets and accelerating innovation - we are reminded today on #EarthDay of the importance of proceeding with caution. A sustainable, circular energy revolution is critical to transforming lives and our global economies, reducing carbon emissions, improving air quality, and preserving our natural resources.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #EarthDay #SustainableEnergy #RenewableEnergy #ClimateAction #GoGreen

Delighted to have joined the opening panel of “Advancing a Just Energy Transition Through Multilateral Action”, hosted by New America  alongside Dr. Chola Milambo, Permanent Representative of Zambia to the United Nations, and moderated by Heela Rasool-Ayub.
 
At a time of rising tariffs, deepening debt burdens, and widening divides in global finance, we face a series of fundamental questions: who defines the energy transition, who benefits from it, and how do we deliver justice at scale?
 
Here are three key messages discussed:

1️⃣ A just energy transition is not a choice, it is a human right: Energy powers health, education, and livelihoods. Nearly 60% of healthcare facilities in 46 low- and middle-income countries face unreliable power. Access to energy is access to life-saving services.
 
2️⃣ Access is no longer just about electricity, it’s about security: Only 2% of global clean energy investment reaches Africa. We need systems that deliver fit-for-purpose finance, debt reform, and de-risking mechanisms that allow countries to drive transitions that advance social protection, gender equality, and local development.
 
3️⃣ Digital and energy systems must be inclusive: AI, data infrastructure, and clean tech depend on critical minerals from the Global South. Yet the value often flows elsewhere. We must build shared digital infrastructure, ensure technology transfer, and promote governance that keeps value local and communities strengthened.
 
At UNDP Sustainable Energy Hub  Energy Hub, we are committed to partnering with countries to deliver transitions that are inclusive, intelligent, and rooted in development priorities. From COP30 to the G20 to FfD4, the path forward must be country-led, digitally enabled, and development-aligned.
 
#EnergyForDevelopment #JustTransntion #AccessForAll

Today, I joined fellow experts and practitioners at the Think7 Summit panel on "Energy Security and Climate", hosted by the Centre for International Governance Innovation (CIGI).
 
Climate change and energy security are deeply interlinked. While the global energy system fuels development, it also drives climate change, accounting for 75% of greenhouse gas emissions. As climate change intensifies, the links with energy security deepen. With conflicts, debt, and rising inequalities straining economies, the G7 has a strategic opportunity to support a just, inclusive energy transition that ensures no one is left behind:
 
➡️ Energy security is climate resilience. Despite record growth in renewables, climate disruptions in 2023 slashed wind energy output by up to 30% and hydropower by over 50% in some regions. Our energy systems must be designed for the climate of today - not the past.
 
➡️ Securing energy means rethinking how and where we invest. Over 90% of clean energy growth is in advanced economies and China, while SIDS face climate losses up to 9% of GDP and unsustainable debt. Through innovative tools like Debt Swaps for Energy, UNDP is helping unlock renewable investment - turning fiscal constraints into opportunities for resilience.
 
➡️ Digital, data, and AI are the new core of energy infrastructure. With electricity demand set to double by 2050, climate intelligence - from predictive models to smart grids - is essential to build resilient, investable, and future-ready energy systems.
 
Now is the time for the G7 to move from ambition to implementation. With 1.18 billion people still living in energy poverty, energy security must drive human development through partnerships, stronger Global South-North cooperation and targeted investment.

🇺🇳 Five years ago the world was in lock-down. The UN helped get us our freedom back and save lives. So why aren’t we celebrating this?👇🏼

Rewind back to 2020. Airports were closed, restaurants were shuttered, many of us were at home, while medical, transport and other key workers were risking their lives. 

We wondered if the world would ever be the same. Yet within two years, restrictions were mostly lifted.

What we saw was an extraordinary coordination effort. Among the key players:
👉🏼 The WHO tracked the spread of the pandemic, shared data and best practices and kept the world informed. 
👉🏼 The US set up Operation Warp Speed to trial different vaccine approaches, fast track approvals, and mobilise pharmaceutical companies with forward contracts. It was joined by other governments and the EU. The WHO facilitated global approval. 
👉🏼 The UN system coordinated vaccine purchase and rollout to developing countries. This included GAVI, UNICEF, UNHCR, peacekeeping and many others. A pandemic isn’t over until it’s eliminated from all countries. 
👉🏼 The UN internally coordinated a rollout to staff in 152 countries: https://lnkd.in/die-DUuN

Of course it wasn’t perfect. 
👉🏼 Risks had to be taken and mistakes were sometimes made.
👉🏼 The tone and language around masks and vaccines from all sides became tribal and divisive. 
👉🏼 Governments were sometimes heavy-handed, which eroded trust.
👉🏼 People in developing countries felt they were being sent the least desired vaccines.
👉🏼 The issue became a geopolitical punching bag. 

But the proof of success is in the pudding. The world returned to normal much faster than expected and governments cooperated both bilaterally and through UN organisations. 

I’m sure I’ve missed a lot here so please feel free to add. 

It was a traumatic time with job losses, separated families and deaths. But let’s not let memories fade on this extraordinary achievement for which colleagues worked hard.

Achieving universal electricity access by 2030 will cost USD 30 billion a year: But how do we get there?
 
While renewable energy investment in Africa grew 96% annually between 2010–2020 - outpacing global trends - the region still received just 2% of global renewable investment over two decades, with over 90% concentrated in a handful of countries. 
 
To close the energy access gap, it is estimated that Africa will require USD 25 billion annually. But public finance alone will not close the gap. Unlocking Africa’s energy future will require:
 ➡️ Deep sectoral reforms — with 58% of African utilities failing to recover operational costs, many remain financially unviable.
 ➡️ Cost-reflective tariffs and revenue certainty — essential to creating a stable investment climate.
 ➡️ Policy reforms — to allow private electricity providers to compete with state-run utilities.
 ➡️ Blended finance models — combining concessional capital with policy reform to de-risk and mobilize private investment at scale.
 
📌 Rwanda’s SEAP program is a strong example: backed by concessional loans, it extended 8,000+ km of power lines, connected 317,000+ new households, and trained 4,000 people — 30% of them women.
 
With the right policies, incentives, and blended finance, sustainable energy access in Africa is possible. The time to act is now - the world cannot afford to leave 685 million people in the dark. 💡

Recent trends such as AI-generated Studio Ghibli images and AI Doll action figures allow users to “cartoonize” their lives. However, these requests impose significant strain on data centres, often leading to infrastructure malfunctions caused by overheating or “melting” due to high demand.

Since OpenAI launched its extended image rendering capabilities in April 2025, over 700 million image generation requests have been made. Unlike “typical” ChatGPT text requests, which consume 2.9Wh, these image requests reportedly consume 3.25Wh. The additional 0.35Wh energy consumption has amounted to over 245 MWh - equivalent to the energy used to power 2,800 10W LED bulbs for a year.

Yet, while servers work overtime to render these trends, 1.18 billion people still live in energy poverty, lacking access to air conditioning, heating, and lighting. This raises a critical question: While AI-generated images are increasing energy demand, how are digital technologies being used to close the access gap for those 1.18 billion energy-poor individuals?

Adopting digital technologies across the energy value chain can accelerate and economize the energy transition through:   
 
➡️ Enhancing efficiency and expanding access to renewable energy sources 
 
➡️ Identifying optimal investment opportunities and enabling informed based decision-making 
 
➡️ “Leapfrogging” traditional energy systems models by integrating more efficient and cost-effective energy solutions  

To learn more about how digital technologies are bridging this energy access divide, I invite you to read this previous edition of the Sustainable Energy Bulletin on Digital, Data, and AI here: 👉 https://lnkd.in/ey4__kbt     #EnergyForDevelopment #AI #EnergyAccess

Grateful to have joined the panel on “Solutions for Clean Cooking to Advance the SDG Agenda”, co-hosted with the Council of Engineers for the Energy Transition (CEET). It was an important space to reaffirm what many of us in sustainable energy for development know well: clean cooking is not a side issue – it is a core pillar of a just and inclusive energy transition. 

Despite major gains in electrification and renewables, 2.1 billion people still rely on firewood, charcoal or dung to cook their meals. This is more than a technical challenge. It is a crisis of equity, health, gender justice, economic productivity and environmental sustainability. 

From the discussion, I emphasized three key action opportunities for scaling clean cooking access within sustainable energy systems: 

🔹 Integrate clean cooking into national electrification and energy access planning from the start. Clean cooking must be positioned as a core energy service – alongside lighting, refrigeration and productive uses – from the outset. This requires incorporating cooking energy demand into load forecasts, tariff design, appliance programmes, and rural mini-grid planning. When planning reflects the full needs of households, including cooking, the developmental impacts are significantly amplified. 

🔹 Scale blended finance and market-building instruments to unlock local market development. Despite offering an estimated $2.4 trillion in annual cost savings, clean cooking continues to receive < 1% of global energy investments. This imbalance reflects a broader failure to recognize clean cooking as a viable market. We must shift this narrative and mobilize coordinated public-private investment strategies. 

🔹 Leverage AI, geospatial tools, and smart technologies to enhance access, affordability, and targeting. The same technologies reshaping electricity access can revolutionize clean cooking. Digitalization offers a powerful opportunity to make clean cooking delivery more efficient, demand-responsive and inclusive. 

At UNDP’s Sustainable Energy Hub, we are supporting more than 80 projects across all regions, advancing clean cooking through technology, policy, and local enterprise development. The solutions exist. The time to act is now. 

To learn more about why clean cooking matters, what’s changing, and how we can scale solutions across the energy transition, I invite you to subscribe to the Sustainable Energy Hub’s bulletin: 👉 https://lnkd.in/eJGZ7XXq

Clean cooking needs $8 billion a year to reach universal access – but we’re mobilizing barely a third of that. This isn’t just a funding gap. It’s a development failure.  

As I said early today: “We’re paying trillions of dollars to avoid spending billions." 

At what point do we stop calling this an “investment gap” when the cost of doing nothing is a thousand times higher? 

The numbers speak for themselves: 

➡️ $2.4 trillion – the estimated annual cost of dirty cooking in terms of healthcare, environmental degradation, and lost productivity. 

➡️ $2.5 billion - the total annual investment currently going into clean cooking solutions. That’s not even a third of what’s needed to achieve universal access by 2030. 

This is not an “investment gap.” It’s a missed opportunity to align climate, health, gender equity, and economic development goals through a single intervention. To change the trajectory, we need to shift the financing paradigm. Here are three catalytic approaches leading the way: 

1️⃣ Blended finance: Combining grants, guarantees, and concessional capital to de-risk private investment, reduce end-user costs, and help early-stage enterprises scale. 

2️⃣ Digital pay-as-you-go systems: Leveraging mobile payments and smart tech to improve affordability, enable real-time monitoring, and unlock access to carbon and impact finance. 

3️⃣ Outcome-based financing: Linking investor returns directly to measurable social and health results, shifting focus from inputs to verified impact. 

At UNDP, we’re advancing these models through Financial Innovation Labs, turning clean cooking from a development afterthought into core climate and infrastructure investment opportunities. Let’s de-risk, digitize, and diversify. Clean cooking is not a side issue; it's a frontline solution for sustainable development.  

#EnergyforDevelopment #CleanCooking

1️⃣ Blended finance: Combining grants, guarantees, and concessional capital to de-risk private investment, reduce end-user costs, and help early-stage enterprises scale. 

2️⃣ Digital pay-as-you-go systems: Leveraging mobile payments and smart tech to improve affordability, enable real-time monitoring, and unlock access to carbon and impact finance. 

3️⃣ Outcome-based financing: Linking investor returns directly to measurable social and health results, shifting focus from inputs to verified impact. 

At UNDP, we’re advancing these models through Financial Innovation Labs, turning clean cooking from a development afterthought into core climate and infrastructure investment opportunities. Let’s de-risk, digitize, and diversify. Clean cooking is not a side issue; it's a frontline solution for sustainable development.

Con el fin continuar impulsando soluciones financieras para la transición energética en Cuba, tiene lugar el sexto encuentro de Laboratorio de Innovación Financiera y Energía (LIFE).

En la sesión, se realizó un intercambio con Enilce Leite Melo, coordinadora del Laboratorio de Innovación Financiera de Brasil, como parte de los esfuerzos de este espacio colectivo por acopiar buenas prácticas internacionales que puedan adaptarse al contexto cubano.

El Laboratorio de Innovación Financiera y Energía fue creado a finales de 2024 como espacio técnico para el diseño, pilotaje y monitoreo de innovaciones financieras que permitan generar nuevas fuentes, mecanismos e instrumentos para atraer financiamiento internacional o realizar un mejor uso de los recursos disponibles para la transición energética en Cuba.

En la actualidad el LIFE trabaja en el diseño de pilotos financieros para la transición energética basados en blended finance, créditos de carbono e incentivos financieros locales, a la vez que explora nuevas oportunidades.

El LIFE está liderado por el Ministerio de Energía y Minas, e integrado por el Banco Central de Cuba, el Ministerio de Economía y Planificación, el Ministerio de Ciencia Tecnología y Medioambiente y Grupo Nacional de Universidades para las Fuentes Renovables de Energía y la Eficiencia Energética, con la asesoría técnica del Programa de las Naciones Unidas para el Desarrollo, PNUD.

El espacio da continuidad a iniciativas anteriores desarrolladas con el PNUD, y los resultados de la Conferencia sobre Financiamiento al Desarrollo.

En su desarrollo prospectivo, irá incorporando otros actores clave, nacionales e internacionales, financieros y no financieros, para fortalecer su papel de diálogo multiactor y de co-creación de innovaciones financieras que impulsen la transición energética en el contexto específico de Cuba.

It was a pleasure to join the webinar on clean cooking and to underscore a critical point: clean cooking is still too often viewed as a household issue, when in fact it reflects an entire value chain and a national development ecosystem. The scale of the challenge demands that we move beyond silos, bringing together data, finance, innovation, and policy to drive real impact, especially for women and marginalized communities.

At UNDP  we’re seeing the transformative power of this integrated approach from Tanzania, where geospatial data is aligning stove distribution with forest degradation trends and user feedback, to Kenya and Uganda, where dedicated eCooking tariffs are making electric cooking more affordable and accelerating the shift away from charcoal.

Together, we can scale these examples into systemic solutions, transforming what is possible and changing daily life for the 2 billion people who still lack access to clean cooking.

This conversation is just the beginning. I look forward to continuing our collaboration to place clean cooking at the heart of the global development and energy transition agenda. Thank you.

No one should have to risk their health to cook a meal. Everyday, over 2.1 billion people strain over open fires and inhale smoke just to feed their families. The energy conversation isn’t complete without clean cooking.
 
This is not just about energy, it is a development priority. It’s about health, gender equality, economic opportunity, and climate action.
 
In sub-Saharan Africa alone, nearly 1 billion people lack access to clean cooking - and 20 million more fall behind every year. In Ethiopia, studies show that a 40% subsidy is often needed just to make biogas affordable. Yet infrastructure barriers like limited grid access and LPG distribution make electric and gas stoves unfeasible for many rural and displaced communities. To scale these technologies meaningfully, it is estimated that we need need at least +$4.5 billion annually - compared to the $700 million currently received.
 
But there’s a way forward. Imagine embedding clean cooking into data-driven electrification planning, so that every new grid, mini-grid or appliance rollout simultaneously advances clean cooking:
 
➡️ In Eswatini, minigrids are supporting productive uses and energy-efficient appliances to boost project revenues.
 
➡️ In Zambia, policy roadmaps link electric cooking with productive uses like irrigation and refrigeration.
 
➡️ In Ghana, Haiti, Kenya, Nepal, and Tanzania, pilots show that integrating electric cooking early in minigrid planning improves business viability.
 
Together, we can move clean cooking from the sidelines to the center of global energy and development strategies. 
 
To find out more about this important interconnection, I invite you to read this UNDP policy brief that explores the pathway to universal clean cooking through integrated, data-powered energy transitions 👉 https://lnkd.in/enecbh7p

Renewable energy is not just a climate imperative - it’s a precondition for digital economies and inclusive growth. 

By 2030, AI is projected to create nearly +170 million new jobs. However, with so many of these new roles yet to be formed, the question remains: how can we connect millions of job-seeking youth to this expanding sector? 

For countries with large youth populations, this isn’t a disruption; it’s an opportunity to build more equitable, future-ready economies. It all starts with energy. AI models and digital tools depend on reliable electricity, yet only 48% of people in Sub-Saharan Africa have access. With 70% of the region under 30yrs, the path forward is clear: renewable energy is the foundation for digital inclusion and youth-led innovation. The solutions are already here: 

➡️ Distributed solar power is enabling rural innovation hubs in Papua New Guinea, where youth and women are launching businesses and learning technical skills. 

➡️ In Indonesia, the Youth Co:Lab initiative supports youth-led enterprises delivering solar cold storage and clean cooking to last-mile communities. 

➡️In Uruguay, a public-private AI training program is scaling in public schools - preparing students for careers in energy, agriculture and logistics. 

➡️In the Dominican Republic, a national AI strategy is helping youth gain digital skills and launch small enterprises. 

Local innovation ecosystems must bridge the gap between energy, data, and jobs. Countries that invest in distributed renewable energy, open-source data platforms and localized AI training programs are better positioned to build domestic markets for AI-enabled services. 

This is not just a development challenge; it’s a strategic opportunity. With the right investment in energy, skills, and ecosystems, we can drive the AI and clean energy transitions from the ground up. To find out how, I invite you to explore the latest edition of the Sustainable Energy Bulletin: 👉 https://lnkd.in/e28kqP-R
